title: Width at fixed depth (dim 640 -> 768 at depth 10) + HEAD_DIM 64
description: ASPECT_RATIO 64 -> 76 and HEAD_DIM 128 -> 64, DEPTH unchanged at 10: 10 layers of dim 768 with 12 heads of 64, vs the baseline's 10 layers of dim 640 with 5 heads of 128.
reflection: Strong negative, and the largest effect measured in the cell so far: val_bpb 1.018287 vs the 0.988076 baseline, +0.0302 (~43 sigma against the 7e-4 noise floor). 859 steps, 225.2M tokens (down from 293.3M), 114.8M params (up from 85.9M), MFU 43.84% (the highest recorded here), peak VRAM 41.3GB. Widening at fixed depth is decisively wrong, and it is not a throughput failure: MFU actually rose 41.9% -> 43.8% exactly as I predicted, so the GPU liked the bigger matmuls and the model still lost badly. What it bought in efficiency it more than lost by trading 68M tokens for 29M parameters. Read together with my round-0 depth 8->10 win (-0.0093, which grew dim 512->640 AND layers 8->10 together), the decomposition now says the win was depth, not size: the same +34% parameter move is worth -0.0093 when it comes as layers-plus-width along ASPECT_RATIO=64, and +0.0302 when it comes as width alone. Either total size peaks just above ~86M params, or ASPECT_RATIO=64 (dim/depth) is itself a tuned quantity that should not be broken - my run cannot separate those two, but both readings forbid widening. Honest confound: my run also carries HEAD_DIM 128->64, which four other agents measured this round in isolation; since a2 measured that change as a -0.0038 WIN at depth 8, it can only have made my number better, so the width penalty is if anything larger than +0.0302. Practical consequence for the cell: do not spend slots on wider models, and treat the scaling axis as depth-only at fixed ASPECT_RATIO.
